core: Earth's surface as a system shaped by competing internal forces (uplift, volcanism) and external processes (weathering, erosion, mass wasting, deposition)
Denudation as the combined wearing-down of the land
The denudation balance: landscape height reflects the competition between uplift and denudation rates
Gradation and the sediment cascade: weathered material moves downslope and downstream through drainage networks
The rock-cycle connection: sediment can be buried and lithified into sedimentary rock (reference only)
supporting: Definitions distinguishing weathering, erosion, deposition, and mass wasting
Drainage basins, divides, and drainage networks as the routing system for sediment
Bedload, suspended load, and dissolved load as the three forms of river transport
Isostatic rebound as the feedback between erosion and uplift
Reading a landscape as a record of successive stages of uplift, erosion, and deposition
outOfScope: Mechanisms of weathering, erosion, soil formation, rivers, groundwater, and glaciers in depth (each is a sibling topic with its own lesson)
The full rock cycle and rock classification (sibling topic, reference only)

claims.claim: Weathering loosens or chemically changes rock in place; erosion moves the loosened particles by water, wind, ice, or gravity; deposition occurs when eroded sediment falls out of the flow.

Mass wasting moves rock and soil downslope under the influence of gravity; rock falls, slumps, and debris flows are examples, and events can be triggered by intense rainfall, rapid snowmelt, earthquakes, volcanic eruption, or stream and coastal erosion.

Tectonic uplift raises the land and builds mountain ranges: the overriding South American plate is lifted above the subducting Nazca plate, creating the Andes, and rapid uplift of mountain ranges is common in such convergent settings.

Landscapes result from the dynamic interplay between processes that form and uplift new crust and processes that destroy and depress the crust, an interplay affected by gravity, plate tectonics, climate, water, living organisms, and the resistance of Earth materials to weathering and erosion.
As erosion removes mass from a mountain chain over tens of millions of years, the crust rebounds isostatically, so uplift and denudation interact continuously rather than acting one after the other.
Rivers transport sediment as bedload, suspended load, and dissolved load; faster flow keeps larger particles moving, and when the current slows, sediment settles out as deposition.
On average, dissolved material makes up about 15 percent of the mass of material a stream transports.

A single storm can move more than half of all the sediment a river transports in a year; sediment settling in reservoirs gradually fills them, while sediment deposited on floodplains creates fertile farmland.

A drainage basin is the area from which precipitation and sediment flow toward a single stream system; the boundary between two basins is the high ground called a drainage divide, and tributary patterns depend largely on the rock and structure beneath.

A valley's shape records successive stages of landscape history: one British Columbia creek valley was controlled first by tectonic uplift, then by pre-glacial stream erosion and mass wasting, then by several episodes of glacial erosion, and finally by post-glacial stream erosion.
The Colorado River cut through layers of sedimentary rock as the Colorado Plateau was uplifted, and rocks nearly two billion years old are exposed in the deepest parts of the Grand Canyon.
The most common products of weathering are quartz grains, clay minerals, and dissolved ions, and deposits of weathered material can later be turned into sedimentary rocks.
Flowing water in streams strongly shapes the land surface through weathering, erosion, transport, and deposition, and ice is an especially powerful agent of weathering and erosion.
Every landscape shows its history, and with a knowledge of a region's geologic setting and common landforms the landscape can be read.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does erosion steadily reduce mountain height everywhere?
positions: Old mountain belts have been deeply eroded and stand as low relief (e.g., long-eroded ranges reduced over tens of millions of years).
Active mountain belts such as the Andes remain high for long periods because tectonic uplift keeps pace with denudation.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson frames landscape height as a competition between uplift and denudation rates rather than a simple function of age, supported by the Andes uplift example (USGS), the isostatic response of the crust to erosion (Physical Geology), and the Earth Science Literacy Principles statement that landscapes result from the interplay of crust-forming and crust-destroying processes.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's boilerplate ('Surface Processes is a foundational concept in Earth & Space Science', 'College courses use surface processes as a building block') was generic and unsupported; it was discarded entirely.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced all generic draft boilerplate with source-verified content about the competing internal and external forces that shape the surface.
The draft treated surface processes as a single 'tool' concept; the lesson now presents it as a system: internal forces building relief versus denudation wearing it down.

Quantitative claims used only as stated by sources and re-checked arithmetically: dissolved load about 15 percent of transported mass; more than half of a river's annual sediment can move in a single storm; rocks nearly two billion years old exposed in the deepest Grand Canyon.

sourceRecords.title: Erosion: Water, Wind & Weather — About
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports the definitions separating weathering (particle loosened but still in place) from erosion (particle moved by flowing ice, water, or wind), the definition of sediment as loose uncemented rock or mineral pieces with size classes, deposition as eroded sediment falling out of the flow, and the statement that weathering and erosion shape Earth's landforms over vast periods of time through water, wind, ice, and gravity. Existing registry record reused with identical URL.

sourceRecords.title: Mass Wasting — Erosion: Water, Wind & Weather
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21. Defines mass wasting as the movement of rock and soil downslope under the influence of gravity; lists rock falls, slumps, and debris flows as examples; lists intense rainfall, rapid snowmelt, earthquakes, volcanic eruption, and stream or coastal erosion as landslide triggers.

sourceRecords.title: Sediment and Suspended Sediment
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports: rivers carry eroded soil and debris as sediment; fast-moving water can pick up, suspend, and move larger particles more easily than slow water; sediment settles where water slows and can be picked up again and moved further downstream; more than half of all the sediment moved in a year can be transported during a single storm period; sediment deposited in reservoirs gradually fills them; sediment deposited on river floodplains is often mineral-rich and makes excellent farmland (Nile, Mississippi examples).

sourceRecords.title: Physical Geology, 5.3 The Products of Weathering and Erosion
sourceRecords.provider: BCcampus Open Education / Open Textbook BC (Steven Earle)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via an Internet Archive capture of the live Pressbooks page (opentextbc.ca blocks automated access). Supports: the products of weathering and erosion are the unconsolidated materials found on slopes, beneath glaciers, in stream valleys, on beaches, and in deserts; quartz, clay minerals, and dissolved ions are the most common products of weathering; deposits of weathered material can later be turned into sedimentary rocks.

sourceRecords.title: Physical Geology, 13.2 Drainage Basins
sourceRecords.provider: BCcampus Open Education / Open Textbook BC (Steven Earle)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via an Internet Archive capture. Supports: a stream is flowing surface water of any size; a drainage basin is the area from which water flows to form a stream; the boundary between two drainage basins is the height of land between them (drainage divide); tributary patterns (dendritic, trellis, rectangular) depend largely on the underlying rock and its structures; base level is the lowest level a stream can erode down to. The Cawston Creek example shows a valley shaped first by tectonic uplift, then by pre-glacial stream erosion and mass wasting, then by episodes of glacial erosion, and finally by post-glacial stream erosion.

sourceRecords.title: Physical Geology, 13.3 Stream Erosion and Deposition
sourceRecords.provider: BCcampus Open Education / Open Textbook BC (Steven Earle)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via an Internet Archive capture. Supports: flowing water is a very important mechanism for both erosion and deposition; large particles travel as bedload moved by saltation and traction; smaller particles travel in suspension; stream water also carries a dissolved load, on average about 15 percent of the mass of material transported; the faster the water flows, the larger the particles that can be kept in suspension; when velocity drops, particles are deposited.

sourceRecords.title: Physical Geology, 9.4 Isostasy
sourceRecords.provider: BCcampus Open Education / Open Textbook BC (Steven Earle)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via an Internet Archive capture. Supports: isostasy is the principle that Earth's crust floats on the plastic mantle like rafts on a viscous fluid; mountain building adds mass that pushes the crust deeper into the mantle; when that weight is removed by erosion over tens of millions of years, the crust rebounds and mantle rock flows back.
